## R² - Coefficient of Determination

R-squared - the coefficient of determination - is a value between 0 and 1 that measures the proportion of variation in the dependent variable that can be explained by the independent variable(s) in a regression model. An r-squared of 0 indicates that the model explains none of the variability. An r-squared of 1 means the model explains all of it.

Essentially, the r-squared measures how much better the model's predictions are, than simply predicting the mean of the dependent variable.

### Sums of Squares

* SST - Sum of squares total:

    $SST=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar{y})^2$

* SSR - Sum of squares regression:

    The variability explained by the regression.

    $SSR=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2$

* SSE - Sum of squares error:

    The variability unexplained by the regression.

    $SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat{y}_i-y_i)^2$

$SST=SSR+SSE$

$\large r^2=\frac{SSR}{SST}$

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(10, 100, 10) + np.random.randint(1, 10, 9)
y = np.arange(1, 10) + np.random.randint(1, 10, 9)

weight, bias = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 5))

def sub_graph(n):
    plt.subplot(1, 3, n)
    plt.scatter(x, y)
    plt.axline([0, bias], slope=weight, c="orange")
    plt.axhline(np.mean(y), c="gray", linestyle="dashed")

sub_graph(1)
plt.vlines(x, y, np.mean(y), colors="blue")
plt.title("SST")
sub_graph(2)
plt.vlines(x, x * weight + bias, np.mean(y), colors="green")
plt.title("SSR")
sub_graph(3)
plt.vlines(x, x * weight + bias, y, colors="red")
plt.title("SSE")
```

### Interpretation

The coefficient of determination measures the goodness of fit of a regression model. A higher r-squared means the model better fits the data. A drawback of r-squared is that it cannot decrease as more regressors are added to the model. It doesn't indicate whether the independent variables are significant. Actually, r-squared may increase as irrelevant variables are added, due to chance alone.

#### Adjusted R²

The adjusted r-squared addresses this issue. It penalizes the use of insignificant regressors.

$\large r^2_{adj}=1-\frac{(1-r^2)(n-1)}{n-k-1}$

As the number of regressors ($k$) increases, the adjusted r-squared decreases, unless the regressor significantly improves the model's fit.
